The number of cousins of a set \(S\) is the number of matchings in the integer line that cover exactly the elements of \(S\), pairing each with an adjacent element not in \(S\). The structure of \(S\) determines the possible matchings.

If \(S\) contains three or more consecutive integers, or two pairs of adjacent integers, there are no matchings. A maximal block of consecutive integers in \(S\) can have size at most 2. Between such blocks there is at least one integer not in \(S\). When the gap between blocks is at least 2, the blocks form independent components whose matchings multiply. When the gap is exactly 1, the blocks share a candidate neighbor, forming a single component.

A component with a pair (size 2) and some singletons yields exactly 1 matching. A component consisting entirely of \(n\) singletons spaced by exactly one integer (i.e., arithmetic progression with difference 2) yields \(n+1\) matchings.

Thus the total number of cousins is a product of factors of the form \(n_i+1\) (from all-singleton components) and possibly factors of 1 (from components containing a pair). To achieve exactly 4040 cousins with minimal \(|S|\), we use only all-singleton components and factor 4040 into integers \(\ge 2\). The sum \(\sum (n_i) = \sum (f_i-1)\) is minimized by the prime factorization.

\(4040 = 2^3 \cdot 5 \cdot 101\), so the factors are \(2,2,2,5,101\). The corresponding component sizes are \(1,1,1,4,100\). The minimum total number of elements is \(1+1+1+4+100 = 107\).

\boxed{107}
